title: Mind / Brain & Memory
content_html:
Mind / Brain & Memory

Logical and Physical Inseparability

Neuroscience: Mind and memory are inseparable functions of the brain’s physical architecture and dynamics; without memory traces in neural circuits, there is no enduring mind or personal continuity.
Buddhism: Mind and memory are inseparable in lived experience, yet not exhaustively reducible to brain tissue alone; continuity of consciousness can extend beyond one lifetime. The views diverge on scope (strictly neural vs. non‑local), but both treat memory as constitutive of mind.

Neuroscientific View — Inseparable in Brain

Logical Inseparability

  • Mind requires continuity over time → continuity requires memory (encoded changes in neural systems).
  • Disrupt hippocampus → disrupt new episodic memory → disrupt continuity of mind (e.g., H.M.).

Physical Inseparability

  • Memories are stored as synaptic/engram traces (LTP/LTD, spine remodeling).
  • Engram activation can cause recall (optogenetics).
  • Systems consolidation: hippocampus indexes → cortex stores long‑term components.

Buddhist View — Inseparable, but Not Only Neural

Mind as Process & Continuum

  • Mind (citta/vijñāna) is luminous and empty; arises dependently, not a static substance.
  • Ālayavijñāna (storehouse consciousness) retains karmic seeds (bīja) across lifetimes.

Implication for Memory

  • Memory is inseparable from mind’s flow, but its ultimate basis need not be restricted to brain matter.
  • Dialogue with science emphasizes disciplined observation but maintains a non‑reductive view of consciousness.

Synthesis — What Both Perspectives Agree On

  • Constitutive role of memory: No enduring personhood or agency without memory (continuity is memory‑dependent).
  • Process view: Mind is dynamic, not a static “thing” — whether framed as neural dynamics or dependent arising.
  • Trainability: Practices that alter attention/learning (e.g., meditation, cognitive training) can reshape memory processes and subjective experience.

The two frameworks can productively inform each other without collapsing their differences.
